Waste
wāst
v. & n. (to squander or lay desolate; a desolation; rendering Hebrew chorbah, shamem, Greek diaskorpizo, apoleia)
From Latin vastus, empty or desolate. Scripture uses the word for a city in ruins and for a fortune squandered, and answers both with the same promise of rebuilding.

Biblical Definition

Waste is both a state and an act: a place laid desolate, and a substance squandered. Nehemiah names the first when he moves men to build: “Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Nehemiah 2:17). The waste is not accepted as permanent; it is stated plainly and then answered with labour. Isaiah turns the same noun into a promise of restoration on a generational scale: “And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations” (Isaiah 61:4). What was ruined for generations is not beyond rebuilding. The active sense appears in the prodigal, and the verb carries the whole moral weight of the parable's first movement: “the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luke 15:13). Our Lord also records the word being used wrongly, by men who called an act of costly devotion a waste: “Why was this waste of the ointment made?” (Mark 14:4). What indignant men called waste, He called a good work.

Webster 1828 Definition

To diminish by gradual dissipation; to squander; to desolate or lay in ruins; also, a desert or ruined place. Scripture pairs the ruin with the promise of rebuilding, names the prodigal's squandering, and corrects those who called costly devotion a waste.

expand to see more

WASTE, v.t. [L. vastus, empty, desolate.] To diminish by gradual dissipation or loss; to squander; to expend without necessity or use; as, to waste an estate.

2. To destroy in enmity; to desolate; to lay waste; as, to waste a country by fire and sword.

3. To wear out; to consume; as, disease wastes the body.

WASTE, v.i. To dwindle; to be diminished; to be consumed by degrees.

WASTE, a. Desolate; uncultivated; destroyed; ruined; as, waste places.

WASTE, n. The act of squandering; loss; destruction; also, a desert; a region ruined and uninhabited.

Key Scripture

Nehemiah 2:17 — "Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach."

Isaiah 61:4 — "And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations."

Luke 15:13 — "And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living."

Mark 14:4 — "And there were some that had indignation within themselves, and said, Why was this waste of the ointment made?"

Modern Corruption

The word is now applied chiefly to inefficiency, so that costly worship is judged wasteful by the same reasoning the disciples used at Bethany, while genuine squandering of a life is called self-discovery.

expand to see more

Mark 14:4 records the only people in the Gospels who used the word waste about an act of worship, and our Lord contradicted them flatly. The reasoning behind their indignation was impeccable by ordinary standards — the ointment could have been sold and the money given to the poor — and it is precisely the reasoning a church adopts whenever beauty, reverence, and costliness in worship are assessed purely by utility. Scripture does not despise the poor; it commands care for them constantly. What it refuses is the calculation that treats devotion to Christ as an inefficiency to be trimmed.

The opposite corruption renames real waste. The prodigal wasted his substance with riotous living, and a far country full of such young men would today describe the same years as finding themselves. The parable is not sentimental about it: the substance was genuinely gone, the famine was real, and the son came to himself only when he was in want. Yet the same chapter and Isaiah 61:4 together are the answer to despair over it. What has been laid waste for generations may be rebuilt, and the father runs while the son is yet a great way off.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chorbah (a desolation, waste place) and shamem (to be desolate) supply the ruin; Greek diaskorpizo (to scatter, squander) gives the prodigal's act and apoleia (loss, destruction) the disciples' complaint.

expand to see more

Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a waste, desolation, ruin; the “old wastes” to be rebuilt in Isaiah 61:4.

Hebrew shamem (H8074) — to be desolate, appalled; the verb behind the desolations of many generations.

Hebrew charab (H2717) — to be dry, to lie waste; the state of Jerusalem in Nehemiah 2:17.

Greek diaskorpizo (G1287) — to scatter abroad, to squander; the prodigal's wasting in Luke 15:13.

Greek apoleia (G684) — loss, waste, destruction; the word the indignant used of the ointment in Mark 14:4.

Usage

"“Jerusalem lieth waste” — the ruin is named plainly and then answered with building."

"“They shall build the old wastes” — desolations of many generations are not beyond repair."

"“Why was this waste of the ointment made?” — costly devotion looked like waste to reasonable men."
